title: In Good GRACES: Principled Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
claim: Among competing selection scores, ours correlates most strongly with downstream performance and gives the lowest regret when choosing within each family.
layout: 2 panels side by side, grouped bar charts; left compares scores across two datasets, right compares regret across three teacher families; legends inside plots, values labeled on bars
description: Two grouped bar charts sit side by side. The left chart plots Spearman correlation (0 to 1) for four scores: Teacher performance, Loss, G-Vendi (Jung et al.), and GRACE (Ours). Each score has a green GSM8K bar and a blue MATH bar, with the value printed above each bar. The GRACE bars are clearly the tallest, at 0.86 and 0.88, while the baselines range from 0.11 to 0.76. The right chart is titled 'LLaMA-1B training on GSM8K'. It plots performance regret (%) for the same four scores, using purple, teal, orange and pink bars, across three teacher families: LLaMA, Qwen and OLMo. The pink GRACE bars are small in every group, for example 0.27 for Qwen, where G-Vendi spikes to 14.47. The eye goes first to the tall GRACE bars on the left and the tall orange Qwen bar on the right.
caption: \textbf{ \gradcv{} correlates with student performance after distillation on math-related reasoning tasks.} We evaluate \llamaS{} and \llamaM{} students on GSM8K and MATH respectively with 15 teachers across LLaMA, Gemma, Qwen, OLMo, and Phi families. (Left) \textit{\gradcv{} shows the strongest correlation with student accuracy} among four scores---teacher performance, student's loss (before training) on the teacher generations, \gvendi{}, and \gradcv{}. (Right) \textit{\gradcv{} reliably selects near-optimal teachers within each teacher family}, measured by its small teacher-student regret, which is the absolute gap in final performance between the best overall student and that obtained from the teacher chosen by each score. Performance is measured by average accuracy over 16 generations per prompt.
abstract: Knowledge distillation is an efficient strategy to use data generated by large "teacher" language models to train smaller capable "student" models, but selecting the optimal teacher for a specific student-task combination requires expensive trial-and-error. We propose a lightweight score called GRACE to quantify how effective a teacher will be for post-training a student model. GRACE measures distributional properties of the student's gradients without access to a verifier, teacher logits, teacher internals, or test data. From an information-theoretic perspective, GRACE connects to leave-one-out stability of gradient-based algorithms, which controls the generalization performance of the distilled students. On GSM8K and MATH, GRACE correlates strongly (up to 86% Spearman correlation) with the performance of the distilled LLaMA and OLMo students. In particular, training a student using the GRACE-selected teacher can improve the performance by up to 7.4% over naively using the best-performing teacher. Further, GRACE can provide guidance on crucial design choices in distillation, including (1) the best temperature to use when generating from the teacher, (2) the best teacher to use given a size constraint, and (3) the best teacher to use within a specific model family. Altogether, our findings demonstrate that GRACE can efficiently and effectively identify a strongly compatible teacher for a given student and provide fine-grained guidance on how to perform distillation.
